item.title: “The team stopped arguing — and that’s bad news”: the anatomy of a socio-technical conflict
item.content:encoded:
If the product and technical teams have suddenly stopped arguing, don’t be too quick to celebrate. Perhaps they have genuinely learnt to reach agreements, but there is another possibility: the arguments have simply lost their meaning.

I’ve seen the latter scenario play out several times. At first, the engineers raise concerns, arguing about technical debt, architecture or deadlines; then they realise that this doesn’t change the outcome, and gradually fall silent. From the outside, things even seem to improve: fewer arguments, faster planning, easier decision-making. But the problem is that, along with the conflict, important feedback may disappear from the system.

Let’s take a closer look at this particular scenario.

What is conflict?

In everyday terms, “conflict” is usually associated with a dispute, confrontation or even a crisis in relations. We are accustomed to thinking of it as an anomaly to be avoided, but in any complex system where different parties are working towards a common goal, conflict is a natural reaction to the fact that participants view that common goal from different perspectives.

I find Thomas Schelling’s perspective in The Strategy of Conflict particularly relevant here. He deals with situations where the parties are neither pure allies nor pure adversaries: some of their interests coincide, others do not, but they are nonetheless dependent on one another to achieve their own goals. The interaction between product and technical teams is very similar to this.

If we apply this logic to product development, I can see at least three areas where interests regularly diverge:

  • Speed vs. stability. It’s important for the business to get results sooner, whilst engineers need to ensure the next change doesn’t end up costing three times as much. This, in particular, is the classic conflict surrounding technical debt, the nature of which I wrote about in my previous article, Technical Debt: Manage It, Don’t Conquer It.
  • Tactics vs. strategy. Sometimes a hypothesis really does need to be tested within a week, even though a technically sound solution would take a month.
  • Boundaries of autonomy. Who decides exactly what we are building, and who decides how it will be implemented.

These contradictions do not in themselves mean that something is wrong with the company. On the contrary, they are entirely natural, and in practice these three contradictions rarely exist in isolation.

Let’s say a product needs to be launched with new functionality in two weeks. First, we argue about speed and stability: can we afford to make a technical compromise to meet the deadline? Then we discuss tactics and strategy: is this really a temporary solution to test a hypothesis, or is it code we’ll have to live with for the next three years?

And it can all end in a dispute over autonomy: the product side proposes a specific technical approach because it seems the quickest, whilst the engineers, in response, start arguing not about the risks of the decision, but about who actually has the right to make it.

A single product task thus traverses all three dimensions at once. And if there aren’t at least roughly clear rules for each of them, the teams have to negotiate not only the task itself each time, but also how they’re going to reach an agreement in the first place.

Where the problem begins

Problems arise when the parties view this negotiation as a zero-sum game: if the engineers are given time for refactoring, the business loses a feature; if the business pushes through a release, the engineers lose out.

In the short term, this logic even works: you can postpone refactoring, quickly release the required functionality and come back to the problem later. I myself have made such decisions many times, and they were by no means always wrong, but the problem itself begins with the word ‘later’.

If one side repeatedly secures a short-term win at the expense of the other, it is not the specific decision that changes, but people’s behaviour in subsequent negotiations. In product development, we don’t reach an agreement just once: the same people return to the negotiations in the next sprint, then again, and again. That’s why it’s not just who won a particular dispute that matters — what matters is what effect that dispute had on the next one. If my arguments have had no impact ten times in a row, by the eleventh time I’ll most likely simply stop wasting my time on them.

Why we’re doomed to conflict: a systems perspective

I myself once spent two years working in a team that tried to be as ‘business-friendly’ as possible. We avoided arguments, smiled during demos and took pride in our lack of conflict.

The result? The platform gradually stopped evolving technically, and the best senior developers quietly left.

That was when I first seriously wondered whether our ‘peace’ was a sign of healthy collaboration. And it didn’t happen all at once — no one gathered the team and said, ‘From today, we’re no longer going to argue with the business’. It was simply that each subsequent discussion became shorter. Sometimes we agreed because the deadline really was important; sometimes we decided to come back to the issue in the next sprint; and sometimes we just didn’t want to spend an hour on a conversation whose outcome everyone could predict in advance.

That’s precisely why I didn’t see it as a problem for a long time. From the inside, this kind of deterioration doesn’t really look like deterioration — it’s more like the team has finally stopped arguing over every little thing. Weekly compromises add up — each one on its own may be entirely justified, but together they gradually change the behaviour of the system.

And this is where I find it more interesting to look not at individual people, but at the system.

In Thinking in Systems, Donella Meadows shows just how much a system’s behaviour depends on its structure: stocks, flows, delays and feedback loops. If you look at the interaction between the product and technical teams in this way, an interesting picture emerges.

The stabilizing loop

In the simplest scenario, the system itself begins to resist the accumulated problems:

Technical debt grows → changes get more expensive → problems can no longer be ignored → time is finally allocated for stabilization.

Nothing magical here — at some point, the cost of inaction simply exceeds the cost of fixing things. But there’s another loop running alongside it:

We need results faster → we agree to a compromise → we ship faster → that pace becomes the new expectation → the next result is also needed faster.

And here’s the crucial point: no one is obliged to make obviously foolish decisions. Each individual compromise may be entirely justified — which is precisely why this scenario is dangerous. The problem only becomes apparent once enough of these decisions have accumulated.

To test this logic beyond mere textual reasoning, I tried to formalise it in a small simulation. The model, available on GitHub, combines system dynamics with an agent-based model of an engineer and a product manager: technical debt, delivery pressure, the response to engineering signals, and the team’s willingness to keep raising those concerns all influence one another through feedback loops and delays.

The central question of the model is simple: can an organisation appear increasingly coordinated at the very moment when its technical risk is rising? In the simulation, one can see how technical risk and apparent conflict begin to diverge, and also examine how this dynamic is influenced not only by the behaviour of the parties, but also by structural rules such as pre-allocated capacity for stabilisation, an error budget and clear limits on technical autonomy.

Then the team goes quiet

The most interesting part comes next. Engineers raise the same issue several times, but the solution is put off each time — after a while, people come to a perfectly rational conclusion: there’s no point in repeating the argument, and the number of such signals decreases.

For the product side, however, the situation improves: previously, planning meetings were constantly dominated by arguments about architecture, technical debt and risks, but now these have stopped; planning proceeds more quickly, and the roadmap moves forward.

Only the risks themselves haven’t gone anywhere — it’s just that information about them has disappeared, and this is already far more dangerous than the conflict itself.

I’m not suggesting that the more arguments there are, the healthier the team is — that’s clearly not the case. But there’s a fundamental difference between ‘we have nothing to argue about’ and ‘we no longer see the point in arguing’. From the outside, these two states may look the same.

For me, this is the key takeaway: the absence of disagreement in itself says nothing about the health of the system. Sometimes it simply means that one of the feedback channels is no longer working.

And then there’s the problem of time

We make a technical compromise today, but we might not start paying the price for it for another six months, and during that time the context gets lost. When a simple change suddenly takes three weeks instead of three days, the product team sees the problem today, whilst the engineers, in turn, may see its cause in decisions made several quarters ago.

Hence the classic exchange:

“Why didn’t you warn us earlier?” “We did.”

And both sides may be speaking in all sincerity — it’s very easy to slip into mutual recriminations here. The product side sees that the team has slowed down, whilst the technical side sees that the cost of past compromises has finally come to light. The problem is that enough time has passed between the cause and the effect for them no longer to appear as parts of the same decision — and next time, reaching an agreement will be even more difficult.

So what do we do about it?

It is impossible to eliminate conflict, nor is it necessary; the product and technical sides have different areas of responsibility, different contexts and different planning horizons — they will view the same decision differently. The question is this: how can we ensure that these disagreements do not turn into either a constant battle or silence on the part of one side?

Simply calling for ‘better communication’ is not enough. If we have to start from scratch every time to argue about stabilisation time, acceptable technical risk, or who has the final say on the implementation method, we will simply be recreating the same conflict in every subsequent sprint.

We need clear guidelines set out in advance for the very same three areas we started with: speed and stability, tactics and strategy, and the limits of autonomy. Not a one-size-fits-all answer to every dispute, but rather starting points from which the parties can proceed when their interests diverge once again.

How much technical risk are we prepared to take for the sake of speed? At what point do we stop experimenting and return to stabilisation? Where does the product side’s right to determine the outcome end, and the technical side’s right to determine how it is implemented begin?

In Schelling’s terms, it becomes interesting here to talk about focal points — reference points around which the parties can coordinate without having to start every negotiation from scratch. It is precisely these that I wish to explore in the next article.

Sources

  1. Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, Harvard University Press, 1960.
  2. Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer, Chelsea Green Publishing, 2008.

item.title: The Model Proposes. Code Decides.
item.content:encoded:
Seven lessons from building and researching customer-facing AI agents that answer with screens

Much of what gets written about AI agents is about agents that work for the person using them: coding agents, research agents, office assistants. A customer-facing agent has a harder job. The person on the other side is a stranger, the conversation touches real records and real money, and no colleague is reading along to catch a mistake before it reaches them.

We call the version we build an agentic application: a customer-facing agent that answers with screens. After more than a year of building an agent that builds them, these are the key things we’d tell anyone about to put an AI agent in front of their customers, or to buy one.

The diagram below is the architecture we think is right. It is our own synthesis of published guidance, research and what we have seen while building. It isn’t a standard. No published study tests this whole architecture, and most of the individual choices in it have no controlled test on real conversations either. Most of the performance numbers we found come from the company selling the product, so we mark those where they appear.

Read it from the top. A customer’s message enters through a channel, passes identity and policy checks, and reaches the model. The model sits inside a harness, the code that runs it and enforces the limits around it. From there the model can read (bottom right) or propose an action (bottom left). The left column is where people step in, and the right column is how you measure and improve. At the bottom are your systems of record, which hold the truth.

1. The model proposes, code decides

A language model is very good at understanding people and writing back, and it can be talked into things. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) explains why: a model has no inherent distinction between data and instruction. For a customer-facing agent, that means what a customer writes, or what sits on a web page it reads, can change what it does.

The pressure doesn’t have to be technical. Reinforce Labs, a vendor that sells testing by attack (red-teaming), attacked 14 live support bots and checked the results against each company’s own published policy. By its count, 28.5% of its 471 attack conversations ended in a policy violation, and unauthorized commitments such as refunds and price matches appeared at 11 of the 14 bots. It says what worked was social, such as emotional pressure and invented urgency, though it gives no success rate per tactic, and its advice is to prepare for an ordinary annoyed customer and not a hacker. The companies aren’t named and nobody has checked the numbers independently.

So the model shouldn’t be the gatekeeper. It proposes, and deterministic code, which gives the same result every time, decides. Identity, permissions, money and what the agent is allowed to do are enforced in code, against your records. OWASP, a non-profit security foundation, tells teams to test for exactly this: unauthorized tools, the connections an agent uses to read or change something in your systems, are denied even when the model requests them confidently. In a test by Arize, a vendor that sells monitoring tools, a simulated support agent reading order pages planted with instructions pulled another customer’s record in 28 of 100 runs. Once access was bound in code to the logged-in session, the agent still tried in 20 of 100 runs, and none returned data. That was one model, with no repeat runs.

We’d put the check at the moment the action runs, not at an earlier step. One study, on a simulated bank-support benchmark, ran the agent through a fixed workflow and found unauthorized writes no lower than without it, at 4.4% of tasks against 4.3%. The authors think the model can misjudge which step it is on, though they didn’t measure that.

Keep the record of the conversation on your server too, not in the visitor’s browser, where it can be faked. Microsoft’s agent framework documentation warns that a malicious client can inject messages to manipulate the conversation history, and recommends persisting it server-side.

People have a place here too. For high-impact actions, the customer says yes to the exact action (user confirmation), and a person from the business signs off when policy requires it (human approval).

Customers can also arrive through their own AI assistant. In Gartner’s survey they used third-party AI tools about three times as often as a company’s chatbot. The same rule applies: verify who the assistant is, then authorize what it may do.

2. The model knows nothing about your business

A model arrives with general knowledge from its training. It doesn’t know your policies, your catalog or this customer’s account. All it knows about your business is what gets brought to it at the moment of the question, and how you bring it is one of the most important decisions you’ll make.

You will hear that some new technology has replaced RAG, the common approach of finding passages in your documents and adding them to the prompt. We found no controlled test showing that. Each kind of question suits a different method:

  • Live facts, such as an account or an order, come straight from your systems through tool calls, limited to this customer. The case for reading them live and not from a searchable copy rests on freshness, accuracy, permissions and one fewer copy of personal data. It is a strong argument and not a measurement: we found no controlled test comparing the two on customer records.
  • Business numbers, such as what counts as revenue, come from written definitions (a semantic layer) and sometimes from code that computes them. With code computing, tests by dbt and AtScale, both vendors, show 8 to 31 more points of accuracy on the kind of questions a data analyst asks, not on customer conversations, and AtScale compares its best of three runs with a single control run. Whether the code is needed is still argued: AtScale says the math must run in code, and MotherDuck, also a vendor, scored plain-text definitions above a semantic layer in its own rough test. According to dbt, a model writing its own query fails with a plausible wrong number, and its semantic layer fails with an error message. In front of a customer, we’d take the error message.
  • Written knowledge comes from classic RAG, a single search of your documents. It holds up on simple questions: an independent benchmark found basic RAG comparable to or better than systems built on a map of how facts connect, though the result depended on the model.
  • Complex questions often suit agentic retrieval, also called agentic RAG or agentic search, where the agent searches, reads and decides whether to search again. Vendors selling it report large gains on complex questions and small ones on simple questions (AWS: under 5 points on one-step questions). It also costs more and takes longer: Microsoft measured 2.6 to 7.8 times the tokens, the units of text models bill by, and IBM, also a vendor, reports 25 seconds against 3 on its customer-support test. A peer-reviewed study found neither a tuned fixed pipeline nor the agentic version universally better.
  • What a customer said earlier comes from long-term memory, for identified customers only. Memory has a write path, so treat each write as an action that code decides. Varonis, a security vendor, showed text hidden on a web page being written into Copilot Personal’s persistent memory. Microsoft has patched it, with no sign of exploitation.

The order we would invest in is our own reading of all this: first the content, meaning clear business definitions and policy documents without contradictions. Then the procedures and tools that apply them. Only then a better search engine.

3. One agent with written procedures

Our default for a customer conversation is one agent that holds the whole conversation and follows written procedures. We expect fewer points of failure and an easier time understanding what happened, and the customer hears one voice. The procedures are text the business can read and change, with versions, so the agent’s behavior isn’t buried in code.

Vendors don’t agree on what sits behind that voice. Fin and Decagon each described one agent in their launches this fall, and Anthropic’s guidance, drawing on its own deployments, says a single agent with instruction packs it loads when needed (skills) often beat separate helper agents (subagents). Salesforce, Sierra and Zendesk describe several agents working together, and Microsoft, in preview, builds its customer conversation product as multi-agent. All of these are vendors describing their own approach. A study across tasks found that, depending on the task, adding agents ranged from 80.8% better to 70.0% worse, with no customer-service test. So this is a default and not a settled question. A team of agents makes sense when there’s a good reason, and scripted steps make sense where the order must be exact.

4. Agents fail silently

An agent can fail with a confident, well-formed answer. There is no error message, just a wrong answer that looks like a right one. The layers underneath can do the same: Cloudflare, reporting on its own service, counted 155 responses containing other customers’ data that went out marked as successful, while its pre-launch tests looked only at response codes and engine performance, not at what the answers said. Knowing that a system responded tells you little about whether it responded correctly.

That is why we think every customer-facing agent needs an automatic eval process, often called online evaluation when it runs on live traffic. An eval is a repeatable check of whether the agent did the job right. In plain terms:

  1. Sample real conversations.
  2. A language model judges them (an LLM judge), and code checks what the agent actually did.
  3. Compare the result with what happened in your records.
  4. Turn what failed into a proposed fix.
  5. A person from the business approves the fix before it goes live (human in the loop), and it reaches everyone gradually when you have enough conversations to try it on a small share first.

Each step is there for a reason. In the Arize test above, a model judge reading only the final answer caught 5 of the 28 leaks; the 28 themselves were counted by a code check on the tool calls. Models judging models can also share the same mistakes: one independent study found a strong overlap, though its authors say disagreement among human raters may explain part of it, and another found it varies by test. So have people check the judges on your own conversations. Testing against AI-simulated customers isn’t enough either: a study with 451 real people found simulators too cooperative, which inflates success. And keep your test set away from whatever builds or improves the agent: researchers at Sierra, a vendor, and Princeton warn that self-authored tests “encode their own blind spots”.

The last step is the one we hold to on conviction. Several vendors now sell an agent that improves the agent, the few results published are their own, and we found nothing independent. We still think the business should approve what changes, because it is the business’s name on the answer. And an approval only means something if someone actually reads it.

5. Guardrails that guess make mistakes in both directions

Guardrails are the checks around a model, and they come in two kinds. A deterministic guardrail is a rule in code: the same input always gives the same result. A model-based guardrail, often called probabilistic, relies on a model’s judgment, often a score that code compares with a threshold.

The second kind is a guess, so it can be wrong both ways: it blocks things that are fine and lets through things that aren’t. NCSC warns against relying on filters that block known bad content, because an attack can always be rephrased. They help, but you can’t rely on them to stop everything.

This matters more since this fall, when decision models arrived: small models such as TypeSafe’s Jev and OpenAI’s Decisions API that return probabilities over fixed answers and write no text. They are fast and cheap, which makes it tempting to put one at every gate, and they are still guesses. We found no threshold validated beyond the data it was set on for checking whether an answer is backed by its source, researchers at Carnegie Mellon conclude that a threshold must be set on the target workload, and research on language models deciding when to escalate finds they misjudge how likely they are to be right. So each team has to test its thresholds on its own labeled data.

Our rule: anything that must never happen is stopped by an exact rule in code, and that rule acts only on what is never legitimate, so it leaves real customers alone. A model’s score is an extra layer. We’d use it to raise a flag, ask a clarifying question and, if needed, send the conversation to a person, where a wrong guess costs little.

6. A conversation that stayed with the agent wasn’t necessarily resolved

The number people like to show is containment: the share of conversations that stay with the agent and never reach a person. It doesn’t tell you whether the problem was solved. Many vendors now headline a resolution rate instead, but the definitions vary, and at least one major vendor counts a customer who leaves without asking for more help as a resolution.

The freshest independent numbers we found come from customers. In J.D. Power’s 2026 wireless study, of 57,339 customers, AI assistants resolved the request in 48% of phone support cases. Satisfaction was 20 points lower on a 1,000-point scale when an assistant was involved, and rose 83 points when it resolved the request. What customers respond to is whether the problem got solved. Nubank, reporting on five of its own production agents, found satisfaction within about 1 to 10 points of expert human agents for four of them and 23.6 points below for debt management. The gap depends on the job.

So measure outcomes from your own records: was the problem solved, and did the customer come back about it? We found no audited measurement across vendors, so your own numbers are the ones to trust.

And keep a person within reach, with the full context of the conversation, and test that path like any other feature. Gartner’s analyst warns against chatbots becoming containment traps, and in its survey of 3,566 customers only 27% would try a chatbot again after a bad experience. In a survey by Five9, a vendor, trust that AI would solve the problem rose from 26% to 55% when a person was reachable. The law is moving on both disclosure and access: EU rules have required since August 2026 that chat systems tell people they are talking to AI, unless it’s obvious; a new California law gives customers of large businesses a way to reach a person from 2027; and New York City has proposed a rule of its own.

7. Text isn’t the right answer in most cases

We think chat is a good way to ask and a poor way to compare, choose, fill in details or confirm an action. A customer doing any of those doesn’t need a wall of text. They need a screen that fits their question, built at the moment they ask it. That is generative UI.

The evidence so far points this way without settling it. In a study at ACL 2026, 428 annotators preferred generated interfaces to chat by 84% to 12% against one model and 69% to 30% against another, and 76 real users on their own questions split 50.8% to 41.1%. A study from Google researchers found them overwhelmingly preferred over standard markdown answers. Those measure preference and not outcomes, on general questions and freely generated pages. We found no test with a business’s real customers, so “most cases” is our conviction from building and not a measured result.

One design point is worth knowing. The Google team behind one such format and the CEO of CopilotKit, a vendor, describe the most popular approach, the declarative one: the model assembles the page from a catalog of approved screen parts and fills them with data, and anything outside the catalog is caught before it reaches the screen. They note the cost: it is safe for the brand but limits deep customization. We’d take that trade. It is the first lesson again: the model proposes, and code decides what appears.

Check it against what you have

Save the diagram and hold it up against what you’ve built or what you’re being offered. Seven questions will get you most of the way:

  1. On identity, money and what the agent may do, who decides: the model or code?
  2. Where does each kind of answer come from, and what happens when the data is missing?
  3. Can the business read and change how the agent behaves?
  4. How would you find out about a wrong answer nobody complained about, and who approves the fix?
  5. What does each guardrail do when it is wrong?
  6. Beyond containment, how do you know the problem was solved, and how does a customer reach a person?
  7. What does the customer see when text isn’t enough?

We build agentic applications at BranderUX, so we aren’t neutral on any of this, and we’d love ideas for improvements and refinements.

item.title: Is Deep Work Possible Anymore?
item.content:encoded:
Agents made software work shallow. Depth now has to be designed.

In 2022, I wrote an article about deep work: why it matters for software developers and how to design your time to make it possible in asynchronous, distracting environments. Back then, successful deep work was mainly about managing your interaction with the environment. Keep distraction-free focus time. Work with full concentration. The deep–shallow design of a workday was crucial. The work itself was deep. We just had to protect it.

Deep work. Essentialism in asynchronous culture

Now it is not enough. In software development, the nature of the work itself changed. Focus on the task was replaced by delegating it to agents and verifying their output. In the past, software development was intrinsically deep (if you were able to find space for it). Today, it has become intrinsically shallow.

Intrinsically Shallow

A few years ago, a properly designed workday looked something like this. You got a challenging issue: implement a new feature in your system. You found a slot in your calendar. Turned off notifications. Timeboxed the task. Design first, then implementation. All the work is done in high focus on what you read and typed.

Now? You read the ticket description. Sometimes you think a little about the problem. But usually you just prompt and delegate the task to the agent. You’re probably working in auto mode, with crafted permissions, so the agent doesn’t bother you with unnecessary questions. The only thing left to do is wait until you can verify.

But waiting is boring. It’s hard to sit for a few minutes, still thinking about the problem, while the agent does the work on your behalf. So you switch context to a different problem and fire up another agent. Or read something on the internet. Or reply to a friend. Anything. And your deep work is gone.

I don’t think it’s your inability to focus. Delegation and conversation — even with an agent — are intrinsically shallow work. Maybe within one session you can keep your focus on a single topic while tackling a problem with your agent. But in the long run, context switching and distraction become the natural way of working. So the change is not in the design of the day. It’s in the nature of the work. Software is just where agents arrived first. Writers, analysts and designers are next.

Surrender by Detachment

We can say: it is what it is. The way we work now makes us more productive. We deliver more. There’s no going back to the way we worked in the past.

That’s true. But it’s also true that this way of working has side effects.

Deep work, I would say, is the way we grow. I genuinely believe it stretches your mind and improves your skills. So the question is whether we can get better without a stable deep work practice. If we lose it, our skills may not only stop improving. They may deteriorate.

Addy Osmani writes about cognitive surrender: the more coding you hand to agents, the more you risk losing the very skills needed to supervise them. In the short term, we’re faster and more productive. In the long term, we slowly lose the skills that made us experienced engineers. We become more and more detached from the craft — the same craft we need to verify what agents produce. That’s cognitive surrender. It’s how comprehension debt accumulates.

Even if agents can do most of the work — and more of it every year — you still need a skillset to be successful, even if that skillset evolves. Here Be Monsters is a good attempt to map what it looks like.

We’ve probably lost deep work as a natural part of our jobs. So where can we still find it?

Friction by Design

Some people say: “Agents save me time, and I can preserve it for deep work.” It’s a good approach. But it rarely happens on its own. This is the efficiency trap striking again. Improved efficiency doesn’t give us more free time. We just do more work. Our worktime is usually stable; the amount of work is not. The saved time ends up in more delegation and more context switching.

Efficiency traps

So we need to be even more proactive in designing our time. Not to bring the old kind of deep work back into our tasks, but to preserve time for deep work in learning. If your tasks no longer cultivate your skills, you need to find a space in your workday to sharpen them. Reserve 1–2 hours a day in your calendar for learning.

Learning, to be fruitful, needs friction. That’s the opposite of how we work with agents. Friction enforces concentration and focus. Monitoring an agent’s work is frictionless.

Recently, I tried no-AI coding tasks. I built my own Redis and a shell that way. You can still pair with your AI to get hints, but you solve the problem yourself. The agent doesn’t write the code. That forces you to think about the design and weigh the options. It’s the difference between passively watching material and retrieval practice: you have to produce something, not only consume it. And that makes the knowledge more durable. CodeCrafters is a good place to start.

Solving interview questions is also a good way to stretch your mind and develop your knowledge. To understand a new idea, rebuild it from scratch, as small as possible (a loop attributed to Andrej Karpathy), or explain it in plain words until you stop stumbling (the Feynman technique). Both expose the gaps you didn’t know you had.

Don’t take the easy way and delegate. Face the problem, and don’t hand the solution to AI.

An Investment, Not an Escape

Since 2022, my opinion about deep work has evolved a little. The approach should be more contextual. Entrenching yourself in deep work can be harmful — both for you and for the organization. A developer who goes dark for days, while the team waits for reviews and answers, isn’t helping anyone. It needs to be balanced to bring gains both personally and for the company.

We don’t need a whole deep workday back. Most of the day can stay shallow: delegating, verifying, answering the team. But you need some intentional deep slots. It’s a long-term investment in your craft. The same craft you need to verify what agents produce.

item.title: Best RAG Chunking Strategy in 2026? I Benchmarked 5 Methods From New Research
item.content:encoded:
Most RAG dashboards report a number that sounds like success: “the right document was in the top 5.” That is partial recall: at least one relevant passage made it into the context.

Real questions rarely need one passage. They need a rule and the definition it depends on, or a limit and its exception. If retrieval finds one of the two, the model writes a confident answer from half the evidence, and a hit-rate metric scores it as a success.

The metric that catches this is complete-evidence recall. For a question q with evidence spans E(q) and an assembled context C(q):

partial(q)  = 1  if  ∃ e ∈ E(q) : e ⊆ C(q)
complete(q) = 1  if  ∀ e ∈ E(q) : e ⊆ C(q)

Between mid-September and the end of October 2026, several papers attacked this gap from the chunking side. Some optimise chunk boundaries directly, some follow the document’s own structure, and some build a graph over chunks. I implemented the core idea of each one in plain JavaScript and added them as a new page to my browser-native Advanced Local RAG demo: the Chunking Lab.

Everything runs in your tab. There is no server, no API key and no model download. Retrieval is BM25 only, so every number in this post is deterministic and reproducible from a URL. A full run (parse, five chunkers, two retrieval modes, all metrics) takes about 11 ms in Node 22.

The research

QESChunker (arXiv 2610.36557, Oct 27) treats chunking as supervised optimisation. Given question–evidence (QE) pairs, human-written or LLM-generated, it picks the chunk boundaries that maximise how much evidence ends up retrievable. Without overlap, the objective decomposes over chunks and dynamic programming finds the exact optimum in polynomial time. With overlap, the objective is monotone submodular. Exact optimisation is then NP-hard, but greedy selection comes with a (1 − 1/√e) approximation guarantee.

StrucChunk (arXiv 2610.26313, Oct 19) uses the structure the author already wrote. It treats a document as a graph of provisions, never cuts across a clause boundary, resolves cross-references (“see Section 4.2”) before embedding, and fuses BM25 with dense retrieval through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. On LegalBench-RAG, Char-Recall@8 goes from 23.59% to 48.18%. On one corpus, Recall@5 rises from 0.557 to 0.804, and the authors attribute 88% of that gain to chunking alone.

SpectRAG (arXiv 2610.36991, Oct 27) stops treating chunks as independent. It builds a weighted graph over chunks (adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citations), seeds it from hybrid search, propagates relevance, and assembles a context under a fixed token budget. The goal is a context that is relevant, diverse, connected and sufficient.

The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading (arXiv 2610.26951, Oct 18) supplies the diagnosis. Across ten frontier and three open-weight models, retrieval reliably surfaces some of the relevant chunks but not all of the chunks a multi-fact question needs. Chunking also strips the document-level context that resolves references between passages.

Three September papers frame the rest:

  • Pre-retrieval Query Clustering for Adaptive Top-k (arXiv 2609.13489) picks retrieval depth per query cluster, reporting over 36% better F1 and 14% fewer tokens on easy clusters. Context size is a per-query variable.
  • Parser, Chunking, and Embedding Interactions (arXiv 2609.31660) runs a 54-configuration factorial study and finds parser and chunker choices interact, with no single retriever winning everywhere.
  • Re-ranking and Late Interaction Drive Retrieval Quality (arXiv 2609.38473) compares six pipelines over about 464,000 papers and finds the biggest levers after first-stage retrieval. The main demo already has a cross-encoder reranker for that.

The test bed

The corpus is a fictional observatory handbook, deliberately written like a policy document:

Each QE pair stores the question and the exact evidence sentences as strings. The lab maps each evidence string to a character span and to the range of text units it covers, using a binary search over unit start offsets:

const unitAt = pos => {
  let lo = 0, hi = units.length - 1
  while (lo < hi) { const m = (lo + hi + 1) >> 1; if (units[m].start <= pos) lo = m; else hi = m - 1 }
  return lo
}

The parser splits sentences on ., ! or ? followed by whitespace, so "1.2-metre" and "Section 1.3" stay intact. A provision is any heading at level 3 or deeper, or any numbered x.y heading, plus the sentences under it. Each provision records its heading path, for example 1 Definitions › 1.3 Red-light zone.

Fixed conditions for every strategy: chunk length limit L = 450 characters, context budget B = 120 words, the same BM25 (k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, stop-word removal and a light suffix stemmer that strips -s, -es, -ed and -ing from tokens longer than four characters), and the same context assembler.

The five chunkers

1. Fixed window

N characters with a 50-character overlap and step L − 50. This is the tutorial default. It cuts mid-word and mid-sentence.

2. Sentence window

The exact algorithm the main demo uses (chunkDocument() in ragEngine.js). It packs whole sentences up to L characters. When a chunk closes, it backtracks whole sentences from the end until the 50-character overlap budget is used, and those sentences start the next chunk.

3. Structure-aware (StrucChunk-style)

One chunk per provision. A chunk never crosses a provision boundary, and a provision longer than L is split on sentence boundaries. Each chunk gets its heading path as a prefix, and every “Section x.y” reference inside it is resolved at index time by appending up to 320 characters of the referenced provision:

for (const m of C.slice(start, end).matchAll(/Section (\d+(?:\.\d+)+)/g)) {
  const ti = byId.get(m[1])
  if (ti === undefined || ti === pi || seen.has(ti)) continue
  seen.add(ti)
  refs.push({ id: m[1], prov: ti, text: bodyText(provisions[ti], refChars) })
}

An indexed chunk then looks like this:

[2 Access and Arrival › 2.1 Gate hours]
The lower gate opens at 17:00. It closes to arriving vehicles 30 minutes
before the start of the dark window defined in Section 1.1. ...
↳ Section 1.1 Dark window: A dark window is any period of at least 90
minutes between the end of astronomical twilight and moonrise. ...

The rule and the definition it depends on are now one retrievable unit.

4. QESChunker, exact dynamic programme

Treat the document as a sequence of n text units. A segmentation splits it into contiguous chunks, each at most L characters. The utility of a chunk covering units j..i−1 is:

u(j, i) = Σ_{e ∈ spans}     1[ e ⊆ [j, i) ]
        + Σ_{q ∈ multi-ev}  1[ ∀ e ∈ E(q) : e ⊆ [j, i) ]
        − μ                                   (μ = 0.05, a small per-chunk cost)

The first term rewards evidence sentences kept intact. The second rewards keeping all of a multi-fact question’s evidence together. The objective is a sum over chunks, so the optimum satisfies a simple recurrence:

best[0] = 0
best[i] = max_{j < i, span(j, i) ≤ L}  best[j] + u(j, i)
for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
  for (let j = i - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
    const span = U[i - 1].end - U[j].start
    if (span > L && j < i - 1) break
    const v = best[j] + util(j, i)
    if (v > best[i]) { best[i] = v; arg[i] = j }
  }
}

The inner loop stops as soon as a window exceeds L, so the cost is O(n · w · |QE|), where w is the maximum number of units per window. On this document the optimum has an objective of 13.35, and every training evidence span stays intact.

5. QESChunker, overlapping greedy

With overlap allowed, the lab picks a set of possibly overlapping windows under a total index budget of 1.35× the document length. The coverage function counts newly covered evidence spans, newly completed multi-fact questions, and α = 0.02 per newly covered unit, so the whole document gets indexed. It is monotone submodular, so the lab runs cost-benefit greedy:

while (true) {
  let bestC = null, bestR = 0
  for (const c of cands) {
    if (spent + c.cost > budget) continue
    const g = gain(c)           // marginal coverage given what is already chosen
    if (g <= 0) continue
    const r = g / c.cost        // benefit per character
    if (r > bestR) { bestR = r; bestC = c }
  }
  if (!bestC) break
  chosen.push(bestC); spent += bestC.cost
  // mark spans, questions and units covered by bestC
}

One practical detail mattered. Without a floor on window size, cost-benefit greedy collapses into one-sentence chunks, because a single evidence sentence has the best gain per character. Candidates shorter than 0.5 · L are therefore excluded. Units still uncovered when the budget runs out are packed into gap chunks so they stay searchable.

The two retrieval modes

Flat top-k

Rank chunks by BM25, then fill the word budget in rank order. The assembler skips any chunk that would overflow the budget and any chunk whose tokens are less than 30% new (a near-duplicate filter that matters for overlapping chunkers):

for (const i of order) {
  const c = chunks[i]
  if (used + c.words > budget) continue
  const t = toks(c.text)
  const novel = t.filter(x => !seen.has(x)).length / Math.max(1, t.length)
  if (picked.length && novel < 0.3) continue
  picked.push(i); used += c.words
  t.forEach(x => seen.add(x))
}

Note the continue rather than break: a large chunk that does not fit lets a smaller, lower-ranked chunk take the space. That detail explains one of the results below.

Chunk graph (SpectRAG-lite)

Build an undirected weighted graph over chunks with four edge types:

Then run personalised PageRank from the top-3 BM25 seeds, with the restart vector weighted by BM25 score, restart probability 0.5 and 25 iterations:

p₀[i]   = s[i] / Σ_seed s          for the 3 seeds, 0 elsewhere
p ← 0.5 · p₀ + 0.5 · Wᵀ D⁻¹ p      (25 iterations)
score[i] = 0.6 · s[i]/max(s) + 0.4 · p[i]/max(p)

The final ranking blends normalised BM25 with normalised PageRank mass and goes through the same budgeted assembler. The only thing that changes between modes is the order in which chunks are offered.

What each chunker builds

Before retrieval, the index itself already says a lot:

Every chunker keeps every evidence sentence intact somewhere, because the sentences are short compared with L = 450. That means all differences below come from findability, not from broken evidence. The columns that differ are granularity, alignment with headings, and whether cross-referenced definitions travel with the rule.

Result 1: Partial recall flatters

Held-out questions, L = 450, B = 120 words:

Every strategy finds something for 69–92% of questions. The default chunkers assemble the whole answer less than a quarter of the time. A pipeline evaluated on partial hits would look healthy while three out of four multi-fact answers were built on incomplete evidence.

The “avg context words” column shows a second effect. The windowed chunkers leave 30–48 words of the 120-word budget unused, because the next-ranked 60–70-word window does not fit. Small chunks pack the budget more efficiently.

Result 2: Structure wins when context is scarce

Provision-sized chunks average 285 characters, against about 400 for the windowed chunkers. At 120 words you can fit two or three provisions but only one large window. When the answer lives in two places, two small, precise pieces beat one big piece that happens to hold half the answer.

The budget sweep (held-out, flat retrieval, L = 450) makes the trade-off visible:

At 40 words, structure-aware is the only strategy above 10%. By 300 words the big-window chunkers have caught up, and by 400 they have passed it, while structure-aware levels off at 77%. With a generous budget, almost any chunker eventually drags the evidence in, because you are sending a large share of the document. The best chunker depends on the budget, and the right budget depends on the query, which is the adaptive top-k paper’s argument from the other direction.

The structure-aware plateau at 77% is not a chunking failure. Its remaining misses are retrieval failures (see Result 5).

Chunk-size sweep

Holding B = 120 and varying L shows the same mechanism from the other side:

Two things stand out:

  1. Structure-aware is flat at 62–69%. Almost every provision is shorter than 450 characters, so L barely changes its chunks. Its granularity comes from the document, not from a hyperparameter.
  2. At L = 800, fixed and sentence windows score 0%. An 800-character window is about 130 words, which is larger than the 120-word budget, so the assembler cannot fit a single chunk. This is the failure you get when chunk size and context budget are tuned by different people.

At L = 250, every chunker gets better and the gap narrows. Smaller chunks behave more like provisions. The cost is a larger index and more fragments for any reader that needs surrounding context.

Result 3: The provably optimal chunker came last

QESChunker’s exact DP is optimal for its objective. It still scored 15% on held-out questions and 58% on the twelve questions it was trained on, below plain fixed windows at 75%.

The boundary map shows the mechanism. The utility function rewards evidence sentences that sit fully inside a chunk, and says nothing about the text around them. The cheapest way to keep a rule intact is to cut immediately before it. In a handbook, the line immediately before a rule is its heading, ### 5.2 Emergency kit. The heading ends up at the end of the previous chunk, and the rule starts the next one. Evidence intact: 100%. But a keyword query about "emergency kit" now matches the chunk holding the stranded heading, not the chunk holding the rule. That is why the DP has 0% of chunks starting at a heading.

Ablation: does a heading-path prefix rescue it? The lab can prefix every chunk from every chunker with the heading path of each provision it touches (the “contextual headers” toggle). Result, held-out, flat:

It does not rescue the DP. The prefix tells BM25 which provision a chunk belongs to, but the chunk holding the stranded heading also gets that provision’s name in its prefix, so both chunks still compete for the same query. The prefix also spends budget words on every chunk. Only the overlap variant, whose windows already tend to start at headings, gains from it.

This is not a flaw in the paper. QESChunker is evaluated with a fixed hybrid retriever, and dense embeddings are far less sensitive to where a heading lands. It is a lesson for anyone porting the idea: the optimisation objective has to model the retriever you actually run. Intact evidence and findable evidence are different goals, and a chunker only optimises the one you write down. A practical fix is to add a term to u(j, i) that scores whether the training question retrieves the chunk under your real retriever, or to forbid cuts between a heading and its first sentence.

The overlapping variant shows the other side. Overlap lets the greedy pass choose windows that start at the heading and cover the evidence. It reaches 46% held-out and 83% on training questions, without being told the document had structure. On documents without clean headings (transcripts, email threads, scanned PDFs), this is the version I would reach for. The training/held-out gap, 83% against 46%, is the caveat for every supervised chunker: the index is shaped around the questions you thought to ask.

Result 4: The chunk graph helps where definitions are hubs

Switching to graph retrieval moved structure-aware chunking from 62% to 69% and changed little else.

One question shows where that gain comes from:

“Is flash photography allowed on the dome floor?” needs two facts: the camera rule (§4.3, flash is banned everywhere in the red-light zone) and the definition (§1.3, the red-light zone covers the dome floor). Flat BM25 ranks the definition third. At 52 words it no longer fits after the first two picks, so the assembler’s continue lets a shorter, useless chunk about the telescope take the space.

In graph mode, the §1.3 definition chunk is a hub: two other provisions cross-reference it, and it shares vocabulary with several more. PageRank mass flows into it from the seeds, its blended score passes the telescope chunk, and the answer becomes complete.

Ablation: turn off cross-reference resolution. Structure-aware graph mode drops from 69% back to 62%, the same as flat. The graph gain comes from the xref edges, which are the most trustworthy edges a document provides.

On windowed chunkers, the graph does not help and sometimes hurts. Sentence windows go from 23% to 15%. Lexical edges between large, mixed-topic windows mostly spread relevance to the neighbours of what was already found. With 40% of the final score coming from PageRank, a neighbour can outrank a correct BM25 pick and take its place in the budget. SpectRAG’s own abstract notes trade-offs in early precision and domain dependence, and this toy reproduces that.

Result 5: What none of them fixed

“My 8-year-old is coming. What rule applies on the terrace?” Every strategy misses both evidence sentences. The rule says “children under 10” and the question says “8-year-old”. After tokenisation the question is [8-year-old, com, rule, appli, terrace], and the rule sentence shares none of those tokens. Structure-aware chunking gets part of the way: the resolved §1.3 reference brings "terrace" into the children's chunk, so it scores 1.18 instead of zero. But "terrace" also appears in several other provisions, and they outrank it. No chunking strategy can close the gap between "8-year-old" and "under 10". That needs a dense or hybrid retriever, query rewriting, or a reranker that understands the question.

This is why the lab complements the main pipeline rather than replacing it. The main pipeline has MiniLM embeddings, hybrid fusion and a cross-encoder reranker. Chunking decides what can be retrieved. The retriever decides what is retrieved. This month’s papers are mostly about the first half of that sentence.

What I would actually do

  1. Measure complete-evidence recall, not hit rate. Write 20 multi-fact questions for your corpus, mark the evidence sentences, and track how often all of them reach the context. Report it next to partial recall. The gap between the two is the number to watch.
  2. If your documents have structure, chunk on it. Split on headings and numbered clauses, prefix the heading path, resolve explicit cross-references at index time. It is deterministic, cheap and explainable, and here it was the biggest single win.
  3. If they don’t, use a supervised chunker with overlap. Generate QE pairs with an LLM, optimise boundaries against them, evaluate on different questions, and put your real retriever into the objective, or at least forbid cuts between a heading and its first line.
  4. Tune chunk size and context budget together. Plot complete recall against budget for each chunk size. If a chunk can exceed the budget, it can never be retrieved. If the curves cross, your “best chunker” depends on how much context you send, and that should vary per query.
  5. Add a chunk graph only where edges are trustworthy. Cross-references, citations and section hierarchy are good edges. Lexical similarity between large chunks mostly is not.

Try it

  • Chunking Lab: vishalmysore.github.io/advancedRagDemo/chunking.html. Change chunk size and budget, switch retrieval modes and splits, toggle heading prefixes and cross-reference resolution, inspect any question, or paste your own markdown and QE JSON.
  • Full RAG pipeline (hybrid search, reranking, WebLLM): vishalmysore.github.io/advancedRagDemo
  • Code: github.com/vishalmysore/advancedRagDemo. The engine is src/utils/chunkLab.js, about 500 lines of dependency-free JavaScript. runLab(text, qe, { L, budget, evalSplit, headers, resolveRefs }) returns every number in this post, so you can run it in Node as well as in the browser.

Every configuration here can be opened from a URL. For example, chunking.html?mode=graph&q=7 opens the flash-photography case in graph mode.

Caveat: this is a toy. One 5,348-character fictional document, 25 questions, BM25 only. Each held-out question is worth about 7.7 percentage points, so one-question differences are noise. The value is in seeing the mechanisms the papers describe: stranded headings, budget crossovers, chunks that cannot fit, definition hubs. The rankings are not a benchmark. Run it on your own documents; that is what the paste box is for.

Papers referenced

  • Zhao et al., QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG, arXiv 2610.36557, October 2026
  • Singh, Tripathi & Singh, StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG, arXiv 2610.26313, October 2026
  • Sahinoglu et al., SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop RAG, arXiv 2610.36991, October 2026
  • Banerjee et al., The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading, arXiv 2610.26951, October 2026
  • Xia, Yamangil & Wang, Pre-retrieval Query Clustering for Adaptive Top-k Document Retrieval in RAG Systems, arXiv 2609.13489, September 2026
  • Singh, Parser, Chunking, and Embedding Interactions in RAG over Indian Government Regulatory Documents, arXiv 2609.31660, September 2026
  • Rathi, Chawla & Andreopoulos, Re-ranking and Late Interaction Drive Retrieval Quality, arXiv 2609.38473, September 2026

item.content:encoded:
0. What Does This Article Answer Next?

The previous article ended by returning to Mutex: it protects an entire critical section, but it allows only one execution unit to enter at a time, regardless of whether that unit reads or writes.

If two threads only read shared state, they do not need to block each other:

Thread A                         Thread B

read counter                    read counter

A read-write lock refines Mutex by distinguishing Readers from Writers:

This article continues with the same two examples:

  • counter++ to see how the Write Lock provides Atomicity;
  • counter + ready to see how Write Lock → Read Lock establishes Visibility and Ordering.

As before, we start with the language-level rules, then trace how the JDK, HotSpot, and the CPU implement them.

1. What Does Java ReadWriteLock Guarantee at the Language Level?

1.1 Atomicity

Java's ReadWriteLock defines the Reader / Writer boundary directly:

“The read lock may be held simultaneously by multiple reader threads, so long as there are no writers.”

It also states:

“The write lock is exclusive.”

Reads may therefore proceed concurrently, while writes remain exclusive.

Use the same counter++ example:

ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
Lock writeLock = rw.writeLock();

writeLock.lock();
try {
    counter++;
} finally {
    writeLock.unlock();
}

With two threads updating concurrently:

Initial: counter = 0

Thread A                         Thread B

writeLock.lock()
                                 writeLock.lock()
                                 wait
read counter -> 0
counter + 1 -> 1
write counter -> 1
writeLock.unlock()
                                 writeLock.lock() returns
                                 read counter -> 1
                                 counter + 1 -> 2
                                 write counter -> 2
                                 writeLock.unlock()

The final value is:

counter = 2

As with Mutex, Atomicity comes from serializing conflicting critical sections under the Write Lock, not from turning counter++ itself into an atomic instruction.

A Read Lock should protect reads only. Multiple Readers may enter together, so it cannot be used to protect shared writes.

1.2 Visibility and Ordering

ReadWriteLock also defines memory synchronization between the Write Lock and the associated Read Lock:

“A thread successfully acquiring the read lock will see all updates made upon previous release of the write lock.”

Use the same counter / ready example:

int counter = 0;
boolean ready = false;

ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
Lock readLock = rw.readLock();
Lock writeLock = rw.writeLock();

// Thread A
writeLock.lock();
try {
    counter = 1;
    ready = true;
} finally {
    writeLock.unlock();
}

// Thread B
readLock.lock();
try {
    if (ready) {
        System.out.println(counter);
    }
} finally {
    readLock.unlock();
}

If B successfully acquires the Read Lock after A releases the Write Lock:

By happens-before:

So once B has acquired the subsequent Read Lock and observes ready == true, the earlier counter = 1 must be visible. This outcome is not allowed:

ready == true
counter == 0

That gives us two guarantees:

  • Visibility: writes completed by the Writer before releasing the Write Lock are visible to a later Reader that acquires the Read Lock;
  • Ordering: the Writer's writes, Write Lock release, Read Lock acquisition, and the Reader's reads form a happens-before order.

2. How Does the JDK Implement ReentrantReadWriteLock?

2.1 Layers

Start with the implementation stack:

2.2 End-to-End Path from Write Lock to Read Lock

Continue with counter / ready: Thread A writes under the Write Lock, then Thread B reads under the Read Lock.

The sequence diagram keeps only the cross-layer path. The Runtime / Language Implementation layer can be expanded into the Reader / Writer contention flow below:

Two counters are encoded in the synchronization state:

In JDK 25, ReentrantReadWriteLock.Sync extends AbstractQueuedLongSynchronizer. Readers use Shared mode; Writers use Exclusive mode; both ultimately contend on the same 64-bit state.

See OpenJDK 25 ReentrantReadWriteLock.java and AbstractQueuedLongSynchronizer.java.

2.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer

2.3.1 Atomicity

Atomicity comes from the state transitions in the flowchart:

A Writer fails if Readers are present or another thread owns the Write Lock.

If the current thread already owns the Write Lock, acquisition is reentrant and increments the exclusive count.

A Reader fails if another thread owns the Write Lock; otherwise it increments the shared count with CAS.

The runtime therefore enforces:

2.3.2 Visibility and Ordering

AbstractQueuedLongSynchronizer stores its state in a volatile long:

private volatile long state;

Its basic operations have these semantics:

Releasing the Write Lock updates state. A later Reader reads and CASes the same state while acquiring the Read Lock:

This is where the language-level Visibility and Ordering guarantees are carried by the Runtime / Language Implementation layer.

2.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer

At the hardware layer, the implementation reduces to the same three capabilities used throughout the series:

compareAndSetState() ultimately uses Unsafe.compareAndSetLong, which HotSpot lowers to an atomic CAS on the target architecture.

Read-write locks add no new hardware primitive. They build the rule “multiple Readers or one Writer” on top of atomic state plus thread waiting / wake-up.

3. How Does the Go Runtime Implement sync.RWMutex?

Go's standard library directly provides sync.RWMutex.

It shares the same core Reader / Writer exclusion model as Java ReadWriteLock: multiple Readers may proceed concurrently, while a Writer must be exclusive. The complete API semantics are not identical.

The most important differences are:

Read-lock reentrancy Java ReentrantReadWriteLock: Supported · Go sync.RWMutex: Recursive RLock is not supported

Write-lock reentrancy Java ReentrantReadWriteLock: Supported · Go sync.RWMutex: Not supported

Write → Read downgrade Java ReentrantReadWriteLock: Supported · Go sync.RWMutex: Not supported

Read → Write upgrade Java ReentrantReadWriteLock: Not supported · Go sync.RWMutex: Not supported

Fairness Java ReentrantReadWriteLock: Optional fair / nonfair mode · Go sync.RWMutex: No fair mode

The Go Memory Model states:

“For any call to RLock, there exists an n such that the n'th call to Unlock ‘synchronizes before’ that call to RLock.”

3.1 Layers

The important distinction from Java is that runtime_SemacquireRWMutex* parks a Goroutine rather than directly blocking one fixed OS thread.

3.2 End-to-End Path from Write Lock to Read Lock

Continue with the same counter / ready example:

var counter int
var ready bool
var rw sync.RWMutex

Goroutine A writes first, then Goroutine B reads:

The sequence diagram keeps only the cross-layer path. The Go Implementation layer can be expanded into the Reader / Writer contention flow below:

The core state is:

See Go's sync/rwmutex.go.

3.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer

3.3.1 Atomicity

Atomicity comes from two core state operations in the flowchart.

A Reader enters through:

readerCount.Add(1)

That update must be atomic. Multiple Readers may increment the count independently.

A Writer first serializes against other Writers through the internal w Mutex, then executes:

readerCount.Add(-rwmutexMaxReaders)

to mark a pending Writer.

The runtime therefore enforces:

Unlike Java, Go does not encode every state in one state word. It combines a Mutex + Atomic Counter + Semaphore to implement the same Reader / Writer rules.

3.3.2 Visibility and Ordering

Go defines RWMutex synchronization at the API level; it should not be inferred from readerCount atomics alone.

The documented relations include:

Using the same counter / ready example:

So once B acquires the Read Lock through this synchronization edge, A's writes under the Write Lock are visible to B in the required order.

Internally, the Mutex, runtime semaphores, and atomic state implement this path. The readerCount.Add operation alone should not be interpreted as synchronizing Readers with one another.

3.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer

At the hardware layer, the implementation reduces to the same three capabilities used throughout the series:

readerCount.Add and readerWait.Add ultimately use the x86-64 atomic-add path. The internal w Mutex reuses the CAS / atomic machinery already covered in the Mutex implementation article.

So sync.RWMutex introduces no new hardware primitive. It combines atomics, a Mutex, and runtime semaphores to implement Reader / Writer semantics.

4. CPython: Why Is There No Read-Write Lock in the Standard Library?

Python is capable of implementing a Read-Write Lock. In fact, CPython had an early proposal to add RWLock to threading: Issue 8800.

The proposal never made it into the standard library. Looking at the long-running Issue 8800 discussion, at least two recurring obstacles stand out.

1. Under traditional CPython, the GIL limited the benefit of a Read-Write Lock

A CPython developer summarized the problem directly:

“since the GIL serializes everything anyway, this isn't likely to benefit many situations”

The basic trade-off was:

So even if multiple threads could acquire the Read Lock together, they usually could not execute Python code in parallel.

RWLock was not useless: I/O and C extensions that release the GIL could still benefit. But for general CPython threading, its advantage was much less direct than in Java or Go.

Free-threaded CPython changes this point. Without the GIL, multiple Python threads can truly execute in parallel, so concurrent Readers become substantially more valuable.

That changes the first part of the trade-off. But even if the benefit of RWLock becomes clearer, the standard library still faces the second problem: there was no consensus on the API and scheduling semantics.

2. Issue 8800 did not reach consensus on the API or scheduling policy

The discussion had two main classes of disagreement.

The first was the API shape:

one unified RWLock
or
two associated Shared / Exclusive Lock objects

One proposal argued that:

“having two different lock primitives ... would be much more flexible, pythonic”

Others preferred a single RWLock abstraction.

The second was the scheduling policy:

Reader priority or Writer priority?
Fair / FIFO?
May new Readers enter while a Writer waits?
Can a Read Lock be upgraded?
Can a Write Lock be downgraded?

Those choices directly affect RWLock behavior and API semantics, and Issue 8800 never converged on one standard design.

So the obstacle was not implementation feasibility. There was no consensus on which RWLock API and policy the standard library should permanently define.

The current threading standard library still provides Lock, RLock, Condition, Semaphore, Event, and related primitives, but no Read-Write Lock.

The original Issue 8800 proposal itself implemented RWLock by composing a condition variable and a lock.

What Python lacks is therefore a standardized RWLock API and policy in the standard library, not the ability to implement Read-Write Lock semantics.

5. Common Pattern Across the Two Implementations

Strip away the APIs and compare what Java and Go must solve.

5.1 Who Gets In? — Atomically Maintaining Reader / Writer State

5.2 What Happens on Conflict? — Park / Wakeup

5.3 Why Can a Later Reader See an Earlier Writer's Data?

The final problem is the synchronization boundary:

Java implements this boundary through AQLS volatile / CAS state transitions.

Go defines the semantics through RWMutex synchronized-before rules and implements them with its internal Mutex, runtime semaphores, and atomic operations.

6. How ReadWriteLock and Mutex Relate

Both protect critical sections. The difference is whether Readers and Writers are distinguished:

Core problem Mutex: mutual exclusion for a critical section · ReadWriteLock: distinguish read and write critical sections

Atomicity Mutex: entire critical section is exclusive · ReadWriteLock: conflicting operations are exclusive; Readers may coexist

Typical use Mutex: general shared-state protection · ReadWriteLock: read-heavy workloads with real contention in read-side critical sections

A compact model is:

ReadWriteLock is not a “stronger” Mutex.

It refines the exclusion boundary so non-conflicting Readers may proceed concurrently.

7. Next: From Shared Memory to Message Passing

Mutexes, atomics, and read-write locks address concurrent access to shared state. But when execution units only need to exchange tasks, they need not compete directly for the same business state.
